analysis.one_liner: Keeps and expands the IRS's free Direct File tax filing program to every state.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 30, 2025 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee; no committee action, no vote, 2 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Direct File is a free IRS system that lets people in 25 states prepare and file their federal tax return directly on the IRS website instead of buying software or paying a preparer. This bill orders the Treasury Secretary to keep Direct File running and, starting with tax year 2026, to bring all 50 states and D.C. into the program. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of taxpayers who file simple returns. Today the program works only in 25 states; the bill would make free direct filing available nationwide, sparing filers the $50-$200 they often pay commercial software or preparers, and sparing lower-income filers who qualify for free versions but are frequently upsold into paid add-ons. Taxpayers get refunds faster when they file free and direct.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Treasury Secretary to continue operating the IRS Direct File free e-filing system, putting it beyond the reach of any administration that might want to shut it down.
Requires every state and D.C. to participate in Direct File for tax years after 2025, expanding it from 25 states to nationwide coverage.
Direct File lets taxpayers prepare and file federal returns free through a portal on the IRS's website, an alternative to paid software and preparers.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial tax preparation and software companies lose the filing fees of taxpayers who switch to the free government system. The federal budget bears the cost of building and maintaining the program for all states.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tax-prep software companies and the federal budget

drawbacks.text: Direct File handles relatively simple returns; taxpayers with complex situations (itemized deductions, gig income, multi-state income) would still need paid software or a preparer, so the mandate does not eliminate filing costs for everyone.

Building and maintaining a nationwide direct-filing system costs federal money each year, and supporters must defend that spending against the argument that private companies already offer free filing options to many filers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and broad: free filing for tens of millions of Americans and a cheaper path to their refunds. The costs are real but smaller — federal upkeep of the system and lost revenue for tax-prep companies. The main design limitation is that Direct File only serves simple returns, so its reach is narrower than its promise.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and no further action has been taken; it has not received a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes introduced H.R. 4267 on June 30, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The bill requires the IRS to continue implementing Direct File and requires all 50 states and D.C. to participate for tax years beginning after 2025; Direct File currently operates in 25 states.
Two Democratic colleagues cosponsored the bill.
The action history shows no committee markup, hearing, or floor vote after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The commercial tax-preparation industry is better off so far: the free, nationwide government filing alternative it competes with remains limited to 25 states and has no path to becoming law this session.

for.name: Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring the IRS to continue Direct File and expand it to every state.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chairs received the bill at introduction and has taken no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Tax preparation software industry
against.role: Commercial filing and software providers (e.g., Intuit/TurboTax, H&R Block)
against.what_they_did: Has long lobbied against government-provided free filing, which competes with its paid products.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters are Democrats; the Republican-chaired Ways and Means Committee has not acted, and no vote has been recorded on the bill.

industries.industry: Tax preparation software and services companies (TurboTax, H&R Block, and similar providers)
industries.note: Direct File gives taxpayers a free government alternative to paid filing software and preparers; a nationwide mandate threatens a large slice of the consumer tax-prep market. The industry's interest in this bill runs against filers who would otherwise save the filing fees.
The bill makes the IRS the permanent, nationwide channel for direct federal tax filing, locking in the agency's direct-to-taxpayer role that some administrations could otherwise scale back or end.

analysis.trajectory: First-term bills with a handful of cosponsors almost always die in committee, and Ways and Means has taken no action in the months since referral. The bill's best realistic path is as a talking point or an amendment on a larger tax or IRS funding bill, not a standalone vote.
